title: When You'll Believe Anything
supportedClaims: People reach for tidy stories when outcomes are messy, especially in markets where randomness and complexity leave gaps that narrative rushes to fill.
After the fact, the mind prefers a coherent explanation to an honest admission that many things were uncertain, surprising, or partly random.
The practical lesson is to distrust explanatory confidence that arrives faster than evidence and to leave more events labeled uncertain than the crowd prefers.
caution: A narrative vacuum is uncomfortable, which is why resisting false certainty requires discipline instead of just skepticism.
